The particles, which can be just a few tens of micrometers wide, have long been thought to come mostly from comets and asteroids closer to the sun than Jupiter ( SN Online: 3/19/19 ).

  But to determine precisely how long a dust grain has spent traveling space, Keller first needed to know how many tracks a grain typically picks up per year. Measuring that rate required a sample with a known age and known track density — criteria met only by moon rocks brought back on the Apollo missions. But the last track-rate estimate was done in 1975 and with less precise instruments than are available today.

  That means it takes longer for dust flakes to pick up tracks than astronomers assumed. When Keller and Flynn counted the number of tracks in 14 atmospheric dust grains, the pair found that some of the particles must have spent millions of years out in space — far too long to have come just from between Mars and Jupiter.

  “I think it’s incredible if Lindsay Keller has shown that he has pieces of Kuiper Belt dust in his lab,” says planetary scientist Carey Lisse of the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory in Laurel, Md. But more work needs to be done to confirm that the dust really came from the Kuiper Belt, he says, and wasn’t just sitting on an asteroid for millions of years. “Lindsay needs to get a lot more samples,” Lisse says. “But I do think he’s on to something.”

If there is a reservoir of heavy water out in the solar system's hinterlands, understanding how that water got out there and stayed out there will inform models that describe the growth of the planets.

Water consists of two hydrogen [atoms](space.com/atoms-definition-history-facts) and an oxygen atom. What we usually refer to as heavy water is water that contains a heavy isotope of hydrogen. An isotope is an atom that contains the usual number of [protons](space.com/protons-facts-discovery-charge-mass) for that element, but a different number of [neutrons](space.com/neutrons-facts-discovery-charge-mass) . Elements are determined by the number of protons they contain. For example, hydrogen always has just one proton. Ordinary 'light' hydrogen has 1 proton and no neutrons, but its heavy isotopes – deuterium and tritium – contain 1 and 2 neutrons, respectively, in addition to the proton.

However, there's another kind of water that features heavy isotopes of oxygen instead. Ordinary 'light' oxygen is made from 8 protons and 8 neutrons and is hence known as oxygen-16 but some oxygen isotopes can have 9 or 10 neutrons, and we call these isotopes oxygen-17 or -18.

Twelve dust grains caught by high-flying NASA aircraft carry water rich in heavy oxygen and radiation scars from more than a million years in space, pointing to a Kuiper Belt source and helping explain why the Sun's oxygen doesn't match the planets'.

2026-11-19 · By Cosmic Herald Staff

Some of the best samples from the outer solar system don't come back on a spacecraft. They drift down through Earth's upper atmosphere, and high-altitude NASA aircraft pick them up in the stratosphere. According to a new paper in *Science Advances*, twelve of these interplanetary dust particles hold a chemical record of water that reacted with rock somewhere beyond Neptune. That water is unusually rich in the heavy isotopes of oxygen.

The study was led by Lindsay Keller of NASA's Johnson Space Center, working with researchers at UCLA. It addresses a question that has been open for more than a decade: why does the Sun's oxygen look so different from the oxygen in the rocky planets?

## A mismatch the Sun left behind

Oxygen comes in three stable isotopes. Oxygen-16 is by far the most common. Oxygen-17 and oxygen-18 carry one and two extra neutrons, and those are what "heavy" refers to here. In 2011, results from NASA's Genesis mission showed that the Sun is rich in oxygen-16 compared with Earth, Mars and the asteroids, which all carry proportionally more of the heavy isotopes.

That is a strange result. The Sun and the planets formed from the same cloud of gas and dust, so in principle they should share an isotopic signature. Something must have pulled heavy oxygen out of the solar mix and delivered it to the solid material that built the planets.

The leading explanation is carbon monoxide self-shielding, a process thought to have operated about 4.5 billion years ago. The idea is that ultraviolet light breaks apart carbon monoxide molecules in the outer parts of the young solar nebula.

An examination of 12 interplanetary dust particles supports the longstanding but hard-to-prove theory that the Kuiper Belt is home to a reservoir of water that’s rich in “heavy” oxygen. corpus-agent.title: DESTINY model tracks molecular chemistry on uneven, ice-covered grains in interstellar space
corpus-agent.snippet: Interstellar space is the scene of active chemical processes: molecules form there in the gas, but also on the surface of tiny dust grains covered in ice. To better represent what happens on these surfaces, astrophysicists at the University of Liège are proposing a deterministic approach based on Markov chains with absorbing states, a mathematical tool that had not yet been utilized in astrochemistry. The paper is published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.
